baby: Pregnancy is counted from the start of the last period, so {baby} isn't here yet. Your body is preparing a fresh, cosy uterine lining.
mom: This is your period week. Many people start a prenatal vitamin with folic acid now, if their provider agrees.
partner: Cheer on healthy routines together: more sleep, more water, a little less stress.

baby: An egg is maturing in one of the ovaries and gets ready to be released around ovulation.
mom: You might notice clearer, stretchy discharge or a slight twinge on one side as ovulation nears.
partner: Plan something relaxed and fun for the two of you this week. Calm and connection go a long way.

baby: Conception! The fertilised egg divides again and again as it travels toward the uterus. {baby}'s genetic blueprint is already set.
mom: Most people feel nothing yet. A few notice light spotting when the embryo implants.
partner: Nothing to see yet, but this is officially the beginning. A quiet celebration is allowed.

baby: {baby} has implanted and is a tiny ball of cells. The placenta and amniotic sac are starting to form.
mom: A missed period, sore breasts or tiredness might be the first hints. A home test can turn positive around now.
partner: If the test is positive, take a breath together. Ask {mom} how she's feeling and just listen.

baby: {baby}'s heart is beginning to form, along with the neural tube that becomes the brain and spine.
mom: Fatigue, mild cramps and needing the bathroom more often are all common now.
partner: Offer to handle dinner a few nights this week. Tiredness can hit hard early on.

baby: A tiny heart is beating, and buds for arms and legs are appearing. Little dimples mark future ears.
mom: Nausea may start to show up, at any time of day. Small, frequent snacks often help.
partner: Stock plain crackers and ginger tea, and keep strong food smells to a minimum.

baby: {baby}'s brain is growing fast, and hands and feet look like little paddles.
mom: Food aversions, cravings and a heightened sense of smell are very common right now.
partner: Don't take a sudden dislike of your cologne personally. Fragrance-free is your friend for a while.

baby: Fingers and toes are starting to form, and {baby} is making tiny movements you can't feel yet.
mom: Many people have their first prenatal visit around now. Bloating and mood swings are normal.
partner: Ask if you can come along to the first appointment and write down questions together beforehand.

baby: The tail is gone and {baby} looks more and more like a tiny human, with eyelids and ear shapes forming.
mom: Your waistband may feel snug even if you're not showing. Heartburn can make an appearance.
partner: Take over a chore that's become hard for {mom}, like the litter box or heavy grocery runs.

baby: All the major organs are in place and starting to work. {baby} is officially a fetus now.
mom: Blood volume is rising, which can mean visible veins and a little lightheadedness. The NIPT blood test window opens around now.
partner: Learn about the screening options with {mom} so you can decide together what feels right.

baby: {baby} can open and close tiny fists, and tooth buds are forming under the gums.
mom: Nausea often begins to ease for many people toward the end of the first trimester.
partner: The NT scan window is weeks 11 to 14. Help book it and block the time in both your calendars.

baby: Reflexes are developing: {baby} can curl fingers and toes and even make sucking movements.
mom: Energy may start to return. Your uterus is rising above the pelvic bone.
partner: Talk about when and how you'd like to share the news. Let {mom} lead the timing.

baby: {baby} has unique fingerprints now, and vocal cords are forming.
mom: Last week of the first trimester. Some people feel a burst of relief and appetite.
partner: Celebrate making it through the first trimester with a favourite meal, whatever {mom} is craving.

baby: Welcome to the second trimester! {baby} can squint, frown and grimace.
mom: Often called the honeymoon trimester: more energy, less nausea for many.
partner: Plan a babymoon or even just a sunny day out while energy is up.

baby: {baby} can sense light through closed eyelids and is busy practising breathing movements.
mom: A stuffy nose or nosebleeds can come from increased blood flow. Totally common.
partner: Keep a humidifier and tissues handy, and maybe extra pillows for comfy sleep.

baby: Muscles and bones are strengthening, and {baby}'s heart pumps lots of blood every day.
mom: Some people feel the first flutters (quickening) between 16 and 22 weeks.
partner: Ask {mom} to tell you the moment she feels a flutter. You'll feel kicks from outside a bit later.

baby: A protective fat layer is starting to form, and {baby}'s skeleton is turning from cartilage to bone.
mom: Your centre of gravity is shifting. Back aches and round ligament twinges are common.
partner: Offer a gentle back rub at the end of the day. Small gestures mean a lot.

baby: {baby}'s ears are in position and may start to pick up sounds. The anatomy scan window opens.
mom: The anatomy scan usually happens between 18 and 22 weeks. Leg cramps may start at night.
partner: Plan to be at the anatomy scan if you can. It's often the most detailed look at {baby} yet.

baby: A creamy coating called vernix is forming to protect {baby}'s delicate skin.
mom: Dizziness can happen when standing up fast. Rise slowly and stay hydrated.
partner: Refill {mom}'s water bottle without being asked. It counts.

baby: Halfway there! {baby} is now measured crown to heel and is swallowing and practising digestion.
mom: Halfway! Your bump is likely showing, and you may feel more regular movements.
partner: Mark the halfway point with a little ritual: a photo, a letter to {baby}, or a fancy dessert.

baby: {baby}'s movements are getting stronger, and taste buds are developing.
mom: Stretch marks and itchy skin can appear. Moisturiser can feel soothing.
partner: Place a hand on the bump in quiet moments. You may feel your first kick soon.

baby: {baby} can now hear your voice and heartbeat.
mom: You may notice leg cramps and a growing appetite.
partner: Try reading a bedtime story to the bump tonight.

baby: {baby}'s lungs are developing the branches they'll use to breathe, and sleep-wake cycles are forming.
mom: Swollen ankles and feet can begin. Putting your feet up helps.
partner: Make a comfy feet-up spot on the couch and claim it as {mom}'s throne.

baby: {baby}'s face is nearly fully formed, with eyelashes and eyebrows.
mom: The glucose screening test usually happens between 24 and 28 weeks.
partner: The glucose test can mean a long morning wait. Offer to drive and bring a snack for afterwards.

baby: {baby} is filling out with more fat, and hair is growing in.
mom: Heartburn and trouble sleeping may increase. Sleeping on your side with a pillow can help.
partner: Consider a pregnancy pillow as a surprise gift. Your side of the bed may shrink, worth it.

baby: {baby}'s eyes are beginning to open, and the startle response is developing.
mom: Braxton Hicks practice contractions can start: painless tightening that comes and goes.
partner: Learn the difference between Braxton Hicks and real labour signs together so you both feel prepared.

baby: {baby} may get hiccups now, which feel like rhythmic little taps.
mom: Last week of the second trimester. The Tdap vaccine window (27–36 weeks) opens.
partner: Ask your own provider whether you should also get a Tdap booster before {baby} arrives.

baby: Third trimester! {baby} can blink and is dreaming in REM sleep.
mom: Welcome to the home stretch. Many providers start checking in every two weeks.
partner: Start talking about birth preferences together. No need to decide everything yet.

baby: {baby}'s muscles and lungs keep maturing, and the head is growing to make room for the brain.
mom: Kicks may feel stronger and more frequent. Some providers suggest daily kick counts.
partner: Ask {mom} if you can help keep track of movements during your evening wind-down.

baby: {baby}'s brain is developing grooves and wrinkles to hold more brain cells.
mom: Fatigue often returns in the third trimester. Rest whenever you can.
partner: Take over the nursery assembly. Flat-pack furniture is a fine love language.

baby: All five senses are working, and {baby} can turn their head from side to side.
mom: Shortness of breath is common as your uterus presses up toward your lungs.
partner: Slow down your walking pace together and keep outings flexible.

baby: {baby} is practising breathing, swallowing and sucking, and toenails have grown in.
mom: Many babies settle head-down around now. Pelvic pressure can increase.
partner: Install the car seat and get it checked. One less thing to think about later.

baby: {baby}'s bones are hardening, except the skull, which stays soft for birth.
mom: Sleep can be tricky. Short naps and a cool bedroom may help.
partner: Take a turn on night-time tidying and morning routines so {mom} can sleep in.

baby: {baby}'s central nervous system and lungs are maturing quickly.
mom: Blurry vision or swelling should always be mentioned to your provider.
partner: Save your provider's numbers in your phone and plan the route to the hospital or birth centre.

baby: {baby} is running out of room, so movements may feel more like rolls than kicks.
mom: Frequent bathroom trips are back as {baby} settles lower.
partner: Pack your own hospital bag too: snacks, charger, a change of clothes.

baby: {baby}'s gums are firm and lungs are nearly ready. Many babies drop lower in the pelvis.
mom: Weekly visits often start now, and the GBS swab usually happens at 36–37 weeks.
partner: Freeze a few easy meals now. Future you will be grateful.

baby: {baby} is practising for life outside: gripping, blinking and turning toward light.
mom: Early term. Watch for signs of labour like regular contractions or your waters breaking.
partner: Keep your phone charged and stay reachable. Agree on a 'this is it' code word.

baby: {baby} is shedding most of the soft lanugo hair and storing up fat.
mom: Nesting urges are real. So is the need to rest between bursts of energy.
partner: Help with nesting tasks so {mom} can save energy for the big day.

baby: Full term! {baby}'s brain and lungs keep developing right up to birth.
mom: You've reached full term. Any day could be the day.
partner: Text-friendly update templates for family can save you lots of typing later.

baby: Due week! {baby} is ready to meet you whenever they decide.
mom: Only a small share of babies arrive exactly on their due date. Waiting is normal.
partner: Plan gentle distractions: a movie, a short walk, a favourite takeaway.

baby: {baby} is fully ready and still growing nails and hair.
mom: Your provider will likely monitor you and {baby} more closely and talk about next steps.
partner: Be the calm one when family keeps asking 'any news?'. You've got this.

baby: {baby} is more than ready. Your provider will guide you on bringing them earthside.
mom: Most people have given birth by now, with or without induction. Rest and trust your team.
partner: Keep the bags in the car and the snacks topped up. Very soon now.
